title: Forensic Pathologist Salary: Convert Your Hourly Rate to Annual Pay
description: Learn how to calculate a forensic pathologist salary from an hourly rate using the 38-hour week, 52-week year. Includes tax, super, and award rates from Fair Work.
salarySummary: A forensic pathologist's minimum hourly rate is set by the Medical Practitioners Award, and converting to annual pay uses the formula hourly × 38 × 52.

Full-time adult ordinary time earnings across all professions were $2,083.70 per week in May 2026. Forensic pathologists are covered by the Medical Practitioners Award, which sets minimum rates. Actual salaries often exceed award rates due to experience, enterprise agreements, or public sector employment.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my annual salary from an hourly rate?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52 weeks. For a full-time forensic pathologist on a 38-hour week, the formula is: hourly rate × 38 × 52 = annual gross pay. This assumes no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. Use the timesheet tool on this site to do the calculation.

faqs.q: Does superannuation count as part of my salary?

bodyMarkdown:
## Understanding the forensic pathologist salary conversion

If you are a forensic pathologist or considering this career, you may need to convert an hourly rate into an annual salary. Whether you are negotiating a contract, comparing job offers, or planning your budget, the standard method is straightforward: multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52 weeks. This article explains the process using the 38-hour full-time week, the fortnight, tax, and superannuation, with reference to official Australian sources.

## How to convert an hourly rate to an annual salary

The basic formula for annual gross pay is:

**hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

For a full-time employee, the standard week under most modern awards is 38 hours. If you are paid $50 per hour, your annual salary would be:

$50 × 38 × 52 = $98,800

This calculation assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates or allowances, and no salary sacrifice. It is a starting point for estimating your gross income before tax and super.

From 1 July 2026, the National Minimum Wage is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for 38 hours. Casual employees receive a 25% loading, making the minimum casual rate $33.05 per hour. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides [pay guides](/blog) for each award, including the Medical Practitioners Award that covers forensic pathologists.

## The 38-hour week and the fortnight

Most full-time awards define a standard week of 38 hours. This is the basis for the annual conversion. If you work 38 hours each week, your fortnightly gross pay is simply your weekly pay multiplied by two. For example, a weekly pay of $1,900 becomes $3,800 per fortnight. Knowing your fortnightly amount helps with budgeting and comparing to salary offers that are quoted per annum.

If you work part-time or irregular hours, adjust the weekly hours accordingly. The formula still works: use your actual average weekly hours.

## Forensic pathologist salary: what the awards say

Forensic pathologists are medical practitioners and are typically covered by the Medical Practitioners Award 2020 (MA000031). The Fair Work Ombudsman publishes pay guides for this award, which list minimum hourly rates for different classifications. These rates are updated after each Annual Wage Review. The Fair Work Commission’s Modern Awards Pay Database also contains the official minimum rates, allowances, and penalty rates.

Because forensic pathology is a specialised field, actual salaries often exceed the award minimum. Enterprise agreements, public sector pay scales, and experience can push earnings higher. The Australian Bureau of Statistics reports that full-time adult ordinary time earnings across all occupations averaged $2,083.70 per week in May 2026. For a 38-hour week, that equates to an hourly rate of approximately $54.83. However, this is a general average, not a forensic pathologist-specific figure.

To find the exact minimum rate for your classification, refer to the Medical Practitioners Award pay guide on the Fair Work Ombudsman website or use the [reference tables](/data) on this site.

## Tax and superannuation

Once you have your annual gross salary, you can estimate your take-home pay after tax and Medicare. For the 2026–27 financial year, the resident tax rates are:

- Nil on income up to $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

A Medicare levy of 2% generally applies. The tax-free threshold is included. Note that the Medicare levy reduction thresholds used here are from 2025–26, as the 2026–27 figures were not confirmed at the time of preparation.

Superannuation is paid on top of your salary. The super guarantee rate is 12% of your ordinary earnings, up to a maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For example, if your annual salary is $120,000, your employer must contribute an additional $14,400 to your super fund. This amount is not included in your take-home pay. Learn more about [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging).

## Casual loading and other considerations

If you work as a casual forensic pathologist, you are entitled to a 25% loading on top of the minimum hourly rate. The casual loading compensates for not receiving paid leave. When using the [the timesheet](/), check the casual loading box if it applies. Do not type a rate that already includes casual loading; the tool adds it automatically.

Remember that the annual conversion is an estimate. It does not account for unpaid overtime, penalty rates, allowances, or salary sacrifice. For a precise calculation, use the Fair Work Ombudsman’s Pay and Conditions Tool or consult your award.

## Conclusion

Converting an hourly rate to an annual salary is simple: hourly × hours per week × 52. For a forensic pathologist on a 38-hour week, this gives a gross annual figure. Add super on top, deduct tax and Medicare, and you have an estimate of your take-home pay. Always check the relevant award or enterprise agreement for your exact entitlements.
